title_en: The supreme law of the land
body_en:
The United States is a republic: the people hold the power and exercise it through the representatives they elect. The rules of that republic are written down in one document, the Constitution, and everything else in American government flows from it. Written in Philadelphia in 1787 and in force since 1789, the Constitution is the supreme law of the land. Every law Congress passes and every law a state passes must agree with it, and a court can strike down any law that does not.

The Constitution does three things. It sets up the government, dividing it into a legislative branch (Congress), an executive branch (the President) and a judicial branch (the courts). It defines the powers of each part, and just as importantly the limits of those powers. And it protects the rights of the people. The opening words, “We the People,” say where the government’s authority comes from: not from a king, not from the states, but from the people themselves. That idea goes by several names on the test: self-government, popular sovereignty, consent of the governed.

The Constitution can be changed, but only by amendment, and the process is deliberately hard. An amendment must be proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and then ratified by three-quarters of the states. In more than two centuries only 27 amendments have passed. The first ten, ratified together in 1791, are the Bill of Rights. They protect the basic rights of Americans and of everyone living in the United States: freedom of speech, religion, the press, assembly and petition in the First Amendment, and further on the right to bear arms, protection from unreasonable searches, and the right to a fair and speedy trial.

Behind the Constitution stands the Declaration of Independence of July 4, 1776. It did not create a government; it announced that the thirteen colonies were free from British control, and it stated the ideas the new country would be built on. All people are created equal. Everyone holds inherent rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Governments exist to secure those rights and draw their power from the consent of the governed. Those phrases are the Declaration’s, not the Constitution’s, and the test asks which document says what.

A few more ideas run through both documents. The rule of law means that everyone must follow the law: citizens, leaders and the government itself, so that no one is above it. Limited government means the Constitution says what government may do and forbids the rest. Natural rights, equality, liberty and the social contract — the agreement by which people form a government to protect them — are the ideas the test calls the important ones. The economic system that grew up alongside them is capitalism, a free-market economy in which people and businesses, not the state, own property and decide what to make, buy and sell.
keyFacts_en: The Constitution (1787) is the supreme law of the land; it sets up the government, defines its powers and protects the rights of the people.
“We the People” means self-government: power comes from the people (popular sovereignty, consent of the governed).
The Constitution is changed only by amendment; there are 27, and the first ten are the Bill of Rights (1791).
The Declaration of Independence (July 4, 1776) said the colonies were free from Britain and that all people are created equal with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
The rule of law: everyone must follow the law, and no one is above it.
The U.S. economic system is capitalism, a free-market economy.

title_en: Three branches, and why there are three
body_en:
The framers of the Constitution had just fought a war against a king, and they were determined that no one person or group in the new government could become too powerful. Their answer was to split power three ways. The legislative branch, Congress, writes the laws. The executive branch, headed by the President, carries them out. The judicial branch, the courts, explains them and settles disputes about them. This is separation of powers, and it is held in place by checks and balances: each branch has ways to limit the other two.

Congress has two parts. The Senate has 100 members, two from every state regardless of size, serving six-year terms. That equal representation was the Great Compromise of 1787, the deal that persuaded small states to join. The House of Representatives has 435 voting members, divided among the states by population, so California has many and several states have only one. Representatives serve two-year terms, short on purpose, so they must follow public opinion closely. A senator represents all the people of a state; a representative represents the people of one congressional district. Both are elected directly by the citizens they represent. Congress writes laws, declares war and makes the federal budget, and only Congress can declare war.

The President is elected for four years and, since the 22nd Amendment, can serve only two terms. The President signs bills into law or vetoes them, enforces the laws, commands the military as Commander in Chief, acts as chief diplomat and appoints federal judges. The Vice President takes over if the President can no longer serve, and after the Vice President comes the Speaker of the House. The President is advised by the Cabinet: the Vice President and the heads of the executive departments, such as the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury and the Attorney General. Presidents are chosen through the Electoral College, the framers’ compromise between a direct popular vote and selection by Congress.

The judicial branch is the Supreme Court and the lower federal courts. The Supreme Court is the highest court in the country, with nine seats; a majority of five usually decides a case. Justices are appointed by the President, confirmed by the Senate, and serve for life, so that they can decide cases independently of politics. The courts review laws, explain them, resolve disputes about them and decide whether a law goes against the Constitution.

Some powers belong only to the federal government: printing money, declaring war, creating an army, making treaties and setting foreign policy. Others belong only to the states: schools, police, fire protection, driver’s licenses, zoning. The 10th Amendment states the rule: powers the Constitution does not give to the federal government belong to the states or to the people. Finally, the test asks about the people who hold these offices now — the President, the Vice President, the Speaker, the Chief Justice, your senators, your representative, your governor. Those answers change with elections, and this app keeps them current and dated for you.
keyFacts_en: Three branches: legislative (Congress) writes laws, executive (the President) enforces them, judicial (the courts) explains them.
The Senate has 100 members, two per state, serving six years; the House has 435 voting members by population, serving two years.
The President serves four-year terms, at most two (22nd Amendment); the Vice President, then the Speaker, is next in line.
The President signs or vetoes bills, is Commander in Chief and appoints federal judges; the Cabinet advises the President.
The Supreme Court has nine justices who serve for life; five usually decide a case.
Only the federal government may print money, declare war, create an army or make treaties; states run schools, police, fire services and driver’s licenses (10th Amendment).

title_en: What citizens owe, and what they are owed
body_en:
Many rights in the United States belong to everyone who lives here, citizen or not. The First Amendment protects freedom of expression and speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of religion and the right to petition the government, and the Second Amendment protects the right to bear arms. When the test asks for the rights of everyone living in the United States, these are the answers.

Some rights are reserved for citizens. Only citizens can vote in federal elections, run for federal office and serve on a jury. Voting itself has been widened four times by amendment: the 15th Amendment (1870) said a male citizen of any race could vote, the 19th (1920) gave women the vote, the 24th (1964) abolished the poll tax, and the 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18. The test asks you to describe one of these four.

People become citizens in three ways: by birth in the United States under the 14th Amendment, by naturalization — the process you are going through — or by deriving citizenship through their parents under conditions set by Congress. New citizens take the Oath of Allegiance, in which they promise to give up loyalty to other countries, to defend the Constitution and obey the laws of the United States, to serve in the military or do important work for the nation if needed, and to be loyal to the United States. The Pledge of Allegiance, which schoolchildren recite, is a shorter promise of loyalty to the flag and to the United States.

Citizenship comes with responsibilities as well. Paying federal taxes is required by law and by the 16th Amendment; it is how everyone funds the federal government, and federal income tax returns are due by April 15. Men aged 18 through 25 must register for the Selective Service, which is required by law and keeps a draft fair if one is ever needed. Serving on a jury when called is a duty only citizens have.

Beyond duties there is participation. Americans take part in their democracy by voting, joining a political party, helping with a campaign, joining a civic or community group, giving an elected official their opinion, contacting their senators and representatives, publicly supporting or opposing an issue, running for office and writing to a newspaper. The test asks for two examples; vote and run for office are the shortest. And when it asks how Americans can serve their country, any of these count: vote, pay taxes, obey the law, serve in the military, run for office or work for local, state or federal government.
keyFacts_en: Everyone living in the United States has freedom of speech, assembly, religion, petition and the right to bear arms.
Only citizens may vote in federal elections, run for federal office and serve on a jury.
Four voting amendments: 15th (any race), 19th (women), 24th (no poll tax), 26th (age 18).
Citizenship comes by birth (14th Amendment), by naturalization, or by derivation through parents.
The Oath of Allegiance: give up other loyalties, defend the Constitution, obey the laws, serve if needed, be loyal to the United States.
Federal taxes are due April 15; men aged 18–25 must register for the Selective Service.

body_en:
Before any European arrived, American Indians — Native Americans — had lived across the continent for thousands of years. The Europeans who followed came for many reasons: freedom, political liberty, religious freedom, economic opportunity, and to escape persecution at home. Not everyone came by choice. Beginning in the 1600s, Africans were taken from Africa and sold as slaves in the colonies, a system that would last until the Civil War.

By the 1770s thirteen British colonies lined the Atlantic coast: New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. The test asks you to name several, so learn the list. The colonists grew angry at Britain for several reasons: high taxes imposed without any representation in Parliament, British soldiers quartered in their homes, and the lack of self-government. The Stamp Act, the Sugar Act, the Townshend Acts and the Intolerable Acts, the Boston Massacre and the Boston Tea Party all pushed them toward a break.

The result was the American Revolution, the war for independence, fought from 1775 to 1783. Its landmarks: the Battle of Bunker Hill, the Declaration of Independence adopted on July 4, 1776, Washington crossing the Delaware to win at Trenton, the victory at Saratoga, the hard winter at Valley Forge, and the British surrender at Yorktown. Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration; it announced that the colonies were free from Britain and declared that all people are created equal.

The first national government, under the Articles of Confederation, proved too weak, so in 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia at the Constitutional Convention and wrote the Constitution. To win ratification, James Madison, Alexander Hamilton and John Jay wrote the Federalist Papers under the pen name Publius, explaining the new document and arguing for it.

The test asks about four founders by name. George Washington led the Continental Army, presided over the Constitutional Convention and became the first president — the “Father of Our Country.” Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration, served as the first Secretary of State and the third president, doubled the country with the Louisiana Purchase, founded the University of Virginia and wrote Virginia’s Statute on Religious Freedom. James Madison, the “Father of the Constitution,” co-wrote the Federalist Papers and was the fourth president, leading the country through the War of 1812. Alexander Hamilton was the first Secretary of the Treasury, a Federalist Papers author, founder of the First Bank of the United States and an aide to General Washington.

Benjamin Franklin founded the first free public libraries, was the first Postmaster General, helped write the Declaration, invented, and served as a diplomat in France.
keyFacts_en: American Indians lived in America before Europeans; Africans were brought and sold as slaves.
Colonists came for freedom, religious freedom, economic opportunity and to escape persecution.
The colonists fought Britain over taxation without representation, quartered soldiers and the lack of self-government.
Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, adopted July 4, 1776.
The Constitution was written at the Constitutional Convention in 1787; Madison, Hamilton and Jay wrote the Federalist Papers to support it.
Washington: Father of Our Country, first president. Madison: Father of the Constitution. Hamilton: first Secretary of the Treasury. Franklin: first Postmaster General, free libraries.

title_en: A growing country, a divided one
body_en:
In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about fifteen million dollars, doubling the size of the country overnight; Thomas Jefferson was president. Over the century the nation fought four wars: the War of 1812 against Britain, the Mexican-American War of 1846 to 1848, which brought in the Southwest, the Civil War, and the Spanish-American War of 1898.

The Civil War, fought from 1861 to 1865 between the North and the South, was the century’s defining event. Its causes were slavery, economic differences between an industrial North and an agricultural South, and disputes over states’ rights. Its landmarks: the first shots at Fort Sumter, the battles of Antietam, Vicksburg and Gettysburg, Sherman’s March, the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, and the assassination of President Lincoln days later.

Abraham Lincoln, the 16th president, led the United States through the war, saved the Union and delivered the Gettysburg Address. In 1863 his Emancipation Proclamation freed the slaves in the Confederate states; the 13th Amendment, ratified in 1865, ended slavery everywhere. The Civil War is the answer when the test asks which war ended slavery.

Two more amendments followed during Reconstruction. The 14th Amendment (1868) declared that all persons born or naturalized in the United States are citizens, and promised equal protection of the laws. The 15th Amendment (1870) said the right to vote could not be denied because of race — so all men could vote, after the Civil War.

Women would wait another fifty years for the vote, but the movement that won it began in this century. Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott and Lucy Stone organized for women’s rights; Sojourner Truth and Harriet Tubman fought slavery and for women’s rights alike. When the test asks what Susan B. Anthony did, the answer is that she fought for women’s rights and for civil rights.
keyFacts_en: The Louisiana Territory was bought from France in 1803.
Wars of the 1800s: the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War, the Civil War, the Spanish-American War.
The Civil War (1861–65), North against South, was caused by slavery, economic differences and states’ rights.
Lincoln saved the Union and freed the slaves with the Emancipation Proclamation; the Civil War ended slavery.
The 14th Amendment made everyone born or naturalized here a citizen; the 15th gave all men the vote (1870).
Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Sojourner Truth and Harriet Tubman led the women’s rights movement.

body_en:
The United States fought five wars in the 1900s. It entered World War I in 1917, under President Woodrow Wilson, after Germany attacked American civilian ships, joining the Allied Powers against Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria. After the war, in 1920, women won the right to vote with the 19th Amendment.

The stock market crash of 1929 — the Great Crash — began the Great Depression, the longest economic recession in modern history. Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected in 1932 and served through the Depression and most of World War II, the only president elected four times. The United States entered that war after Japan bombed Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, fighting the Axis Powers — Japan, Germany and Italy — alongside the Allies. Dwight Eisenhower commanded the Allied armies in Europe, became the 34th president, ended the Korean War and signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 that created the Interstate System.

After World War II came the Cold War, a decades-long rivalry with the Soviet Union. The United States’ main concerns were the spread of communism and the threat of nuclear war. It fought the Korean War from 1950 to 1953 and the Vietnam War to stop communism from spreading. In 1991 it led the Persian Gulf War to force the Iraqi military out of Kuwait.

At home, the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s fought to end racial discrimination. Martin Luther King, Jr. led it, working for equality for all Americans and for a country where people would be judged, in his words, not by the color of their skin but by the content of their character. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 were its great victories.

On September 11, 2001, terrorists hijacked four planes and attacked the United States, crashing two into the World Trade Center in New York City, one into the Pentagon in Virginia, and one, aimed at Washington, into a field in Pennsylvania. The War on Terror followed, with wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. The test also asks for an American innovation — the light bulb, the automobile and assembly line, skyscrapers, the airplane, the integrated circuit, the moon landing — and for the name of an American Indian tribe, such as the Cherokee, Navajo, Sioux, Apache or Hopi.
keyFacts_en: World War I: entered in 1917 under Wilson after Germany attacked U.S. ships. Women got the vote in 1920 (19th Amendment).
The Great Depression began with the 1929 crash; Franklin Roosevelt was president through it and most of World War II.
World War II: entered after Pearl Harbor (1941) against Japan, Germany and Italy; Eisenhower was a general, later president.
The Cold War rival was the Soviet Union; the concern was communism. Korea and Vietnam were fought to stop its spread.
The civil rights movement, led by Martin Luther King, Jr., fought to end racial discrimination.
September 11, 2001: terrorists attacked the United States; the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq followed.

body_en:
The 2008 civics test has a short geography section; the 2025 test keeps only two of its questions, about the capital and the Statue of Liberty. If you filed your N-400 before October 20, 2025, learn all of it.

The United States lies between two oceans. The Pacific Ocean is on the West Coast, off California, Oregon, Washington, Alaska and Hawaii. The Atlantic Ocean is on the East Coast, from Maine down to Florida. The two longest rivers are the Missouri and the Mississippi, which join near St. Louis and drain the center of the continent to the Gulf of Mexico.

To the north is Canada. Thirteen states border it: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, Minnesota, North Dakota, Montana, Idaho, Washington and Alaska. To the south is Mexico, bordered by four states: California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas. Beyond the fifty states, the United States has five inhabited territories: Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam. Their residents are American citizens (nationals, in the case of American Samoa) but have no senators and a non-voting delegate in the House.

The capital of the United States is Washington, D.C. The District of Columbia is not part of any state; it was created from land given by Maryland so that the capital would belong to the whole nation. The Statue of Liberty, a gift from France dedicated in 1886, stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor, where it greeted millions of immigrants arriving by ship. Both of these questions appear on every version of the test.
keyFacts_en: The Pacific Ocean is on the West Coast; the Atlantic Ocean is on the East Coast.
The two longest rivers are the Missouri and the Mississippi.
Thirteen states border Canada (including Maine, New York, Michigan, Washington and Alaska); four border Mexico (California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas).
The territories: Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, Northern Mariana Islands, Guam.
The capital is Washington, D.C.; the Statue of Liberty is on Liberty Island in New York Harbor.

title_en: The flag, the anthem and the motto
body_en:
The flag of the United States tells the country’s story in two numbers. Its thirteen stripes stand for the thirteen original colonies that became the first states. Its fifty stars stand for the fifty states today, one star for each; the fiftieth was added for Hawaii in 1960. When a new state joins, a star is added on the next Fourth of July.

The national anthem is “The Star-Spangled Banner.” Francis Scott Key wrote the words in 1814, during the War of 1812, after watching the American flag still flying over Fort McHenry in Baltimore at dawn following a night of British bombardment. The song became the official anthem in 1931.

The nation’s first motto was “E Pluribus Unum,” Latin for “Out of many, one.” Chosen in 1782 for the Great Seal of the United States, it originally meant one nation formed from thirteen colonies; today it is read as one people drawn from many origins. It appears on the Great Seal and on American coins. A second motto, “In God We Trust,” was adopted in 1956 and appears on paper money.

Two more symbols appear elsewhere on the test. The Statue of Liberty, a gift from France in 1886, stands in New York Harbor as a symbol of freedom and welcome. And the Pledge of Allegiance, recited facing the flag, is a promise of loyalty to the flag and to the United States — “one Nation, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.”
keyFacts_en: The flag has 13 stripes for the 13 original colonies and 50 stars for the 50 states.
The national anthem is “The Star-Spangled Banner,” written by Francis Scott Key during the War of 1812.
“E Pluribus Unum” means “Out of many, one.”
The Pledge of Allegiance shows loyalty to the flag and to the United States.

title_en: The national holidays and what they mark
body_en:
The United States has eleven national holidays, set by federal law. In calendar order: New Year’s Day on January 1; Martin Luther King, Jr. Day on the third Monday of January; Presidents Day, officially Washington’s Birthday, on the third Monday of February; Memorial Day on the last Monday of May; Juneteenth on June 19; Independence Day on July 4; Labor Day on the first Monday of September; Columbus Day on the second Monday of October; Veterans Day on November 11; Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday of November; and Christmas Day on December 25. The 2025 test asks you to name three of them; the 2008 test asks for two.

Three of these have their own questions, and two of them are easy to confuse. Independence Day, July 4, celebrates the adoption of the Declaration of Independence in 1776 — the country’s birthday, marked with parades and fireworks. Memorial Day honors soldiers who died in military service; it began after the Civil War as Decoration Day, when families decorated the graves of the fallen. Veterans Day honors everyone who has served in the U.S. military, living or dead; it falls on November 11, the day World War I ended in 1918, and was first called Armistice Day. If the question says “died,” the answer is Memorial Day; if it says “served,” the answer is Veterans Day.

The other holidays mark the country’s story too. Martin Luther King, Jr. Day honors the leader of the civil rights movement. Presidents Day honors George Washington, and by custom Abraham Lincoln and all presidents. Juneteenth, made a federal holiday in 2021, marks June 19, 1865, when the last enslaved people in Texas learned they were free. Labor Day honors American workers, Columbus Day the 1492 voyage, and Thanksgiving the harvest feast shared by the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag in 1621.
keyFacts_en: There are eleven national holidays; name three (2025 test) or two (2008 test).
Independence Day, July 4, celebrates U.S. independence — the country’s birthday.
Memorial Day honors soldiers who died in military service.
Veterans Day, November 11, honors everyone who has served in the military.
Juneteenth (June 19) marks the end of slavery; Martin Luther King, Jr. Day honors the civil rights leader.
